**Course:** DOTE5891VM Low Altitude Economics · Second Trimester, 2026–27 · MSc in Aviation Management · CUHK Business School  
**Instructor:** Chiu Yu Ko

Also on this site: [Readings](readings.qmd) · [Lectures](lectures.qmd)

## Description

This course studies the economics and business strategy of the low altitude economy (LAE), including drones, eVTOL aircraft, vertiports, U-space/UTM systems, BVLOS operations, and related finance, insurance, certification, and platform services. The course uses Hong Kong and the Greater Bay Area as the core applied setting, while drawing comparisons with NASA, AiRMOUR, EASA/U-space, FAA/AAM, and global advanced air mobility frameworks.

The course is intentionally quantitative and managerial. Students learn to translate LAE use cases into demand forecasts, unit economics, infrastructure breakeven models, partnership contracts, regulatory roadmaps, airspace mechanisms, ESG/social-license strategies, risk registers, and investment recommendations. Each week connects a business problem to simple but powerful analytical tools, including NPV, value of time, generalized cost, elasticity, HHI, CASK, CPMK, TAM/SAM/SOM, barrier haircuts, Monte Carlo sensitivity, Pigovian tolls and taxes, and network-scaling formulas.

By the end of the course, students should be able to evaluate whether a proposed LAE service is commercially viable, socially acceptable, policy-consistent, and scalable across Hong Kong and the GBA. The capstone presentation requires students to integrate demand, cost, infrastructure, regulation, airspace access, sustainability, and risk into one coherent business or policy strategy.

Attendance requirement: students are required to have at least 70% attendance in this course.

## Objectives

- Study LAE economics and business strategy in Hong Kong and the GBA, with global AAM comparators.
- Build quantitative and managerial tools for demand, unit economics, infrastructure, partnerships, regulation, airspace, sustainability, and risk.
- Integrate those tools into a coherent business or policy strategy (capstone) and exam-ready analysis.

## Learning outcomes

After completing this course, students are expected to:

- Understand demand and supply dynamics in urban air mobility using basic economic models and stakeholder analysis, with a focus on Hong Kong/Greater Bay Area trends.
- Estimate market sizes and evaluate investment decisions through simple cost-benefit analysis and market simulations.
- Explore pricing strategies, economic incentives, and congestion management for sustainability and public acceptance.
- Review business frameworks, value-chain positioning, and regulatory economics, drawing on global case studies from NASA, McKinsey, and AiRMOUR.
- Develop strategies for market growth, policy evaluation, and stakeholder engagement via scenario discussions and team projects.

## Assessment (shape)

| Element | Weight | Details |
|---------|--------|---------|
| Participation | 10% | Case discussions, quick polls, role plays, spreadsheet workshops, bidding games, negotiation exercises, and peer feedback. |
| Assignment | 20% | Short individual or group submissions applying tools such as NPV, HHI, CASK, NASA demand, ROI, certification value, congestion pricing, barrier haircuts, and ESG KPIs. |
| Project | 30% | 12-minute integrated HK/GBA LAE strategy pitch with quantitative core, risk register, regulatory roadmap, sustainability/social-license strategy, and executive memo. |
| Final exam | 40% | Open notes and books. Integrated quantitative and policy-consistent analysis across all course topics. |
| **Total** | **100%** | |

Late submission of assignment would **not** be accepted.

## How the weeks build

From the course outline’s cumulative strategy-building sequence:

- **Weeks 1–3:** Build a basic HK/GBA use case, map the value chain, assess market structure, and construct cost/revenue unit economics.
- **Weeks 4–6:** Extend the use case with demand forecasting, infrastructure ROI, and a commercial partnership or PPP design.
- **Weeks 7–10:** Add regulatory approval strategy, airspace access mechanisms, market-sizing barriers and uncertainty, and sustainability/social-license design.
- **Weeks 11–12:** Deliver the capstone presentation and prepare for integrated final-exam analysis using the master viability framework.
